title: Exomiser's ranking of variants contributed to diagnoses of rare disease in the pilot of the 100,000 Genomes Project
summary: In a pilot of England's National Health Service, Exomiser ranked candidate variants for 2,183 families. A quarter of probands got a genetic diagnosis. A quarter of those were actionable at once.
headline: Exomiser ranks gene variants to help diagnose rare disease in England
metric: Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders
brief: The 100,000 Genomes Project ran a preliminary national study in rare disease. From May 2016 through April 2019, the study returned results to the Genomic Medicine Centers of the English National Health Service. Across 2,183 families, genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands. Clinicians reported that a quarter of the diagnoses could be acted on at once. Exomiser ranked candidate variants against each patient's phenotype. Of the 490 diagnoses based on single-nucleotide variants or indels, 88% were among Exomiser's top five candidates. Of the same diagnoses, 92% were made with the applied gene panels or those candidates.[1] The study's authors report that one diagnosis enabled a curative transplantation of bone marrow for a 10-year-old girl. They also report that another diagnosis let the younger brother of a baby who had died undiagnosed start weekly injections. They do not say whether Exomiser or the applied panels flagged either variant. Neither outcome can therefore be credited to the software. In a later reanalysis across the full project, Exomiser ranked candidate variants again. After manual interpretation of the ranked candidates, diagnoses were found for 463 of 24,015 patients whose cases the earlier analysis had left unsolved. In a separate deployment in Hong Kong, Exomiser ranked 67% of 132 diagnoses first.[2]

brief: In November 2016 a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, had an epileptic seizure. It left her unresponsive and not breathing.[1] Her Embrace wristband detected the seizure and alerted her mother, who called paramedics. The teacher survived. Her rescue rests on a single IEEE Spectrum report. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the device on 26 January 2018, after the event.[2] Later evidence comes from hospital units where patients with epilepsy are monitored. Researchers in Montreal published a study of the device in their own unit on 7 January 2026. They found that the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working. It raised 29 false alarms in 373 days of monitoring. It detected none of 510 focal seizures without convulsions, a type that the device is not cleared to detect.[3]

title: Real-time fall alerts from SafelyYou Guardian's AI video cut residents' time on the ground by about 30 minutes in six California memory care facilities
summary: In six California memory care facilities, real-time alerts from SafelyYou Guardian cut residents' time on the ground after a fall by 29.6 minutes. Its AI detects falls on video.
headline: Camera alerts bring help sooner to residents with dementia who fall
metric: time on the ground fell by 29.6 minutes (95% CI 20.3 to 38.9)
brief: Between May and August 2018, staff in six California facilities that provide memory care received real-time alerts from SafelyYou Guardian. The system uses AI to detect falls on video. In that period, residents with dementia spent on average 29.6 fewer minutes on the ground after a fall than in a baseline period without alerts. That baseline period was November and December 2017. The share of fallers who lay on the ground for more than an hour fell from 31% (8 of 26) to none. In 97.6% of the falls, the resident could not stand up alone. The study compares periods in the same facilities, with no concurrent control group. Every author had ties to SafelyYou.[1] In 2023, authors at Imperial College London included the study in a synthesis of research on video recording for direct patient care. These authors declare no conflicts of interest. They listed the same reductions. In their reading, the reductions show that the system improves care after falls.[2] Video monitoring with AI was tried for a year in two South Australian aged care facilities. False alerts there reportedly overwhelmed staff and contributed to a real event being missed.

deployer: Six memory care facilities in California (not named in the paper)
location: Six memory care facilities, California, United States

comparator_after: No such events in the real-time notification period

metric: the child was recovered within weeks
brief: This case rests on the word of one speaker. In a WIRED report of 19 June 2019, Thorn's chief executive, Julie Cordua, said that a California officer had run a missing child's photo through Spotlight. In April 2019 the officer had seen the photo in a post by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Spotlight, using Amazon's facial recognition, returned a list of online sex ads that featured the girl. She had been sold for weeks. More traditional police work followed. Cordua said that the child was recovered within weeks.[1] No police or court record of the case is among the sources. The gap matters to anyone who cites the story. The figures in Thorn's 2017 impact report came from surveys of its police users. Viral claims have also treated identification as rescue.[2] Amazon Rekognition, which Spotlight used for the face match, has falsely matched members of Congress to mugshots.

location: Hartshorne Woods Park, Middletown Township, New Jersey, United States

deployer: Research sites in 11 countries under a multi-center study with University of Oxford / Mahidol-Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit-affiliated investigators (research use, not routine service)
location: 11 sites in Burkina Faso, Kenya, Republic of the Congo, Senegal, South Africa, Uganda, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Nepal, Thailand and Brazil
case_jurisdictions: Burkina Faso | Kenya | Republic of the Congo | Senegal | South Africa | Uganda | Bangladesh | Cambodia | Nepal | Thailand | Brazil
comparator_against: expert microscopy

headline: Nigeria uses machine-learning poverty maps to direct COVID-19 cash aid
metric: 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 October 2021
brief: Nigeria had no urban social registry. Its National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office therefore built the Rapid Response Register for a government-funded cash transfer during the COVID-19 pandemic. The government used maps of poverty by ward, made by applying machine-learning algorithms to satellite imagery. With them it selected 1,163 of the poorest urban wards, with a population of over 20 million.[1] Their residents then registered by mobile phone and were verified in person. The developers of the maps report that, in targeting the poor, their machine-learning approach raises precision at the ward level to 0.92. A survey-based benchmark reaches 0.79.[2] No source shows how many people the maps helped. A World Bank status report of 29 January 2025 records 49,000 beneficiary households in the cash transfer as of 15 October 2021. The World Bank does not say how many of them had been paid. It also counts over 5 million households supported by the program of direct benefit transfers. It gives no breakdown of the share that the register targeted.[3] Human Rights Watch researchers argued in July 2021 that the targeting methods had in all likelihood excluded, or would exclude, large numbers of people in need.[4]

title: Baricitinib, identified with BenevolentAI's knowledge graph, lowered COVID-19 deaths in the RECOVERY trial
summary: BenevolentAI researchers used the Benevolent Platform's knowledge graph to identify baricitinib for COVID-19, and in the RECOVERY trial mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone.
headline: Drug found with a knowledge graph lowered COVID-19 deaths in a trial
metric: mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone
brief: On 4 February 2020 BenevolentAI researchers reported in The Lancet that their knowledge graph had helped them identify a possible treatment for COVID-19. It was baricitinib, an arthritis drug. In the ACTT-2 trial, 1,033 hospitalized adults received remdesivir with either baricitinib or a placebo. Median recovery took 7 days with baricitinib and 8 days with the placebo. In the COV-BARRIER trial, 8% of patients receiving baricitinib had died by day 28, compared with 13% receiving a placebo. Mortality was a secondary outcome in that trial. The trial did not meet its primary outcome of reduced disease progression.[1] In the later RECOVERY trial, 8,156 patients were randomly assigned to usual care with or without baricitinib. Mortality, its primary outcome, was 12% with baricitinib and 14% with usual care alone.[2] On 14 January 2022 the World Health Organization strongly recommended baricitinib with corticosteroids. The recommendation covered patients severely or critically ill with COVID-19. On 10 May 2022 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved baricitinib for hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who need supplemental oxygen or other respiratory support. The European Medicines Agency reached the provisional opinion that three trials did not conclusively show meaningful benefit. Eli Lilly then withdrew its European application on 7 December 2022.[3] None of the trials compared discovery with AI against discovery without it. The knowledge graph's part in the choice rests on a letter and a methods paper by BenevolentAI researchers.[4]

brief: The Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service called this the first find in Poland of a missing person using a drone and SARUAV.[1] The missing man was 65. He had Alzheimer's disease and had left home in Cergowa a day after a stroke. Police with tracking dogs did not find him after a storm. On 29 June 2021 the rescue service made four drone flights and ran the SARUAV software on 782 images. After 4 hours and 31 minutes of analysis the software returned his coordinates. Rescuers found him unconscious in grass over two meters tall, after more than 24 hours outdoors. They handed him to the ambulance service. Independent authors wrote that each use of the system needs map data prepared for the area. Other independent authors wrote that SARUAV gives no details on its training data or model architecture.[2] SARUAV Ltd. employs three of the five authors of the case report. The Polish press quotes the rescue service's own account of the find and describes the failed ground search.[3]

brief: In October 2021 a 55-year-old man in Jamshedpur, India, had symptoms at work. His Fitbit Sense showed an irregular rhythm at 164 beats per minute. Ventricular tachycardia lies outside the rhythms that it was cleared to classify.[2] The benefit also rests on an assumption that he would have waited longer without the reading. A single case report leaves no way to check it.

brief: On 14 December 2021 WeChat announced an “anti-fraud customer service reminder” for WeChat Pay. WeChat's example was a man in Yunnan, identified only by his surname.[1] ChinaZ reported that the man had met a woman on a video platform. Within a week she asked to borrow 190,000 yuan for medical treatment. As he began the transfer, a voice reminder from WeChat Pay appeared. He then received a call from its customer service. The agent on the call judged from experience that this looked like a dating scam and advised him to cancel.[2] He canceled the payment. The automated step in these accounts is the flagging of a risky transaction. Neither WeChat nor ChinaZ says how this transfer was flagged or whether any model was involved. WeChat and ChinaZ credit the agent's advice with his decision to cancel. No confirmation from the police or a bank is reported. No date is given for the transfer. In September 2022 Xinhua listed the reminder among WeChat Pay's risk warnings. It gave no figures on the reminder's effect.[3]

title: A smartwatch alert for a fast irregular heart rate leads to a defibrillator implant, after which an X-ray shows a lung cancer that surgeons remove
summary: A smartwatch of unstated brand alerted a 58-year-old man to an irregular heart rate above 180 beats per minute. In the care that followed, doctors found a lung adenocarcinoma. Surgeons removed it.
headline: Doctors find lung cancer after a smartwatch flags a fast heart rate
metric: The 35 mm tumor was staged pT2a pN0 M0 with clear margins
brief: Clinicians at St George's Healthcare NHS Trust and East Surrey Hospital in England published a case report on 4 January 2022. They describe how a smartwatch alert led indirectly to a diagnosis of lung cancer. The patient was a previously well 58-year-old man with no smoking history of note. His smartwatch alerted him that his heart rate was irregular and above 180 beats per minute. He felt nothing at the time.[1] In hospital, electrocardiograms captured no meaningful arrhythmia. A cardiologist diagnosed non-sustained ventricular tachycardia from the watch's results. He received an implantable defibrillator. The routine chest X-ray after the procedure happened to show an abnormality in his right upper lung. Further imaging and a biopsy showed an adenocarcinoma, which surgeons removed with clear margins. The cancer lay outside what the watch was built to detect. The authors judge that without the watch the tumor would likely have grown undetected. They also judge that, without the watch, curative surgery might not have been an option.[2] The authors do not name the watch's brand or model. Its alerting algorithm therefore cannot be identified. They give no dates for any of the events. The only follow-up that they report is his discharge on the tenth day after surgery and an outpatient magnetic resonance scan of his heart.

brief: On 20 March 2022 officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at a checkpoint in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged the car. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets of factory-made explosive, 52.5 kg in all. The explosive was assessed as PETN-RDX.[1] The driver was a police officer posted in Istanbul. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. It sentenced four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for the same offense.[2] ASENA was designed to flag drug crime. This find lay outside its purpose. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March 2022 that police had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs. He said that the police had used analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”.[3] The head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department spoke in June 2022. He listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source records the data that ASENA matched for this car. None of the sources says whether an analyst checked the flag before the stop. The driver spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no informant is reported.[5]

brief: A trial in Taiwan tested alerts to physicians from an AI analysis of electrocardiograms. Its primary endpoint was death from any cause within 90 days. At an academic medical center and a community hospital, 15,965 patients were randomly assigned to AI-assisted care or usual care. Ninety-day mortality was 3.6% with AI-assisted care and 4.3% with usual care. The hazard ratio was 0.83, with a confidence interval of 0.70–0.99 at the 95% level. The upper bound lies just below 1, the value of no effect. The research team that developed the system ran the trial.[1] Researchers at Sheba Medical Center later restated the result in a paper on randomized trials of cardiovascular AI. They did not reanalyze the trial's data. They judged that mortality gains across these trials were often modest or reached statistical significance mainly in subgroup analyses.[2] The trial measured fewer deaths with the alert pathway. It does not show which clinical actions made the difference. Longer-term survival remains uncertain. It is also uncertain whether the result holds in other health systems.

title: An early resistance warning helped doctors change a woman’s antibiotic
summary: China Medical University Hospital’s Intelligent Anti-Microbial System flagged ceftazidime resistance in 1 hour. Doctors changed a 78-year-old woman’s antibiotic before she recovered.
headline: An early resistance warning helped doctors change a woman’s antibiotic
metric: flagged ceftazidime resistance in 1 hour
brief: A 78-year-old woman at China Medical University Hospital in Taichung developed severe pneumonia during a prolonged admission. Within an hour, the hospital's Intelligent Anti-Microbial System predicted from a bacterial mass spectrum that her Stenotrophomonas maltophilia isolate resisted ceftazidime. It suggested levofloxacin. Po-Ren Hsueh, a vice-superintendent of the hospital, said that conventional susceptibility testing takes two to three days.[1] Clinicians changed the antibiotic in June 2022. The hospital reported that she recovered and went home in late July 2022.[2] The benefit rests on one patient. Every account of her comes from the hospital and its staff. Researchers with no tie to the hospital published a paper on 30 September 2026. They rated the hospital's own before-after study of the platform at serious risk of bias. They cited its lack of a concurrent control group.[3] The hospital counts more than 100,000 uses of the platform. That count covers the wider service and includes no number of recoveries.[4] The hospital's account supports an earlier change of antibiotic. None of the sources establishes that the prediction saved her life.

domain: Healthcare - clinical microbiology and antibiotic therapy

brief: The ScreenTrustCAD study measured what an AI reader adds where breast screening already uses two radiologists.[1] Karolinska Institutet researchers ran it at Capio Sankt Göran Hospital in Stockholm. From 1 April 2021 to 9 June 2022, Lunit's Insight MMG ran in the background on the screening mammograms of 55,581 women. Two radiologists alone would have found 250 cancers. With the AI as a third reader, 269 were found. In the paired design, two radiologists and the AI read the examinations independently. The 19 extra cancers therefore came from examinations that only the AI flagged.[2] The researchers also found that one radiologist with AI was non-inferior to two radiologists, with 261 cancers against 250. The study ran at one hospital with one mammography vendor. Lunit was among its funders.[3]

headline: Doctors find a pulmonary embolism after Apple Watch records low oxygen

brief: A 50-year-old woman who had recently had COVID-19 was referred to the hospital of Oita University in Yufu, Japan, for breathlessness. Four days before admission, a primary care physician had measured her oxygen saturation at 94 to 98%. Hospital pulse oximetry read 97%. But her Apple Watch Series 7 had shown 88% in the early morning. Prompted by the watch reading, clinicians ordered CT angiography. They diagnosed pulmonary embolism with bilateral deep venous thrombosis. She was treated with an anticoagulant and discharged on day 15. The authors state that the low reading led to the diagnosis.[1] The Blood Oxygen app is built for general wellness. Detecting an embolism lies outside its purpose. In 2023, other authors examined five studies of the Series 6 with 973 patients. They found that the watch shows no strong systematic bias against medical-grade pulse oximeters. They also found that outliers of up to 15 points occur.[2] The case depended on clinicians who acted on a watch reading when the hospital reading was normal.[3]

title: Sepsis alerts from COMPOSER are associated with lower mortality in two emergency departments at UC San Diego Health
summary: After UC San Diego Health deployed COMPOSER, a deep-learning model that alerts nurses to sepsis, mortality was 9.49%, against a modeled 11.39% without it.
headline: Fewer sepsis patients die after COMPOSER alerts UC San Diego nurses
metric: 1.9 percentage points
brief: COMPOSER is a deep-learning model that flags possible sepsis to nurses. It went live in two emergency departments at UC San Diego Health on 7 December 2022. The evaluation covered 6,217 adults with sepsis seen before and after that date. Mortality after deployment was 9.49%, against a modeled 11.39% without COMPOSER. That is an adjusted reduction of 1.9 percentage points, with a confidence interval of 0.3–3.5 at the 95% level. Raw mortality before deployment was 10.3%. The comparison rests on historical controls, with no randomization and no concurrent untreated group. The estimated benefit reached statistical significance at only one of the two hospitals.[1] In a meta-analysis published on 13 May 2025, Yale authors pooled seven randomized trials of other alert systems for sepsis. They found no statistically significant effect on mortality.[2] The COMPOSER team reported in August 2026 that the alerts stayed in use in both emergency departments through October 2025. A large language model was added as a layer in July 2024. The mortality result is an association, reported by the team that built COMPOSER and the health system that deployed it.

developer: University of California San Diego research team
deployer: UC San Diego Health

brief: Lund University researchers ran the MASAI trial within the Swedish national screening program. Between 12 April 2021 and 7 December 2022, they randomly assigned 105,934 women in southwest Sweden to Transpara-supported screening or to a control group. In the control group, two radiologists without AI did standard double reading. The AI group had 6.4 screen-detected cancers per 1,000 women against 5.0 in the control group. It needed 44.2% fewer screen readings.[1] Results for the primary outcome, the rate of interval cancers, appeared in The Lancet in 2026. The rate was 1.55 per 1,000 with AI and 1.76 per 1,000 without. That result met the trial's non-inferiority margin. The difference was not statistically significant.[2] The trial tested one product in one region. Its design does not separate the effect of the triage by risk score from that of the marks on suspicious areas.[3]

brief: Maidstone Borough Council uses an AI-enabled Xantura platform to flag households for proactive homelessness support. In a presentation published on 4 November 2024, a Kent County Council presenter reports that fewer than 1% of flagged households that received support became homeless. The figure was 40% for a group that went without support because the housing team lacked capacity. The groups were not randomized. The comparison does not separate the effect of the targeting from that of the support. The presenter does not date these outcomes.[1] The UK government's National Plan to End Homelessness, published on 11 December 2025, features Maidstone's use of the platform. Its figures for June 2023 to January 2025 include £440,000 saved in temporary accommodation and 96 homelessness cases avoided. No method is stated for them.[2] In June 2026, the Centre for Homelessness Impact was still running a randomized trial of similar data-led outreach with Xantura. That trial covers four other councils. A tool for screening families in a Pennsylvania county also scores households from administrative data. Its scores allegedly fell unevenly on Black families. Kent's presenter states that protected characteristics are not included in the live prediction model.

brief: Operation Renewed Hope ran from 17 July 2023 into early August at the Cyber Crimes Center of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported 311 probable identifications of previously unknown child victims. It also reported several confirmed rescues from active abuse. Arrests had already been made in the United States and Canada.[1] The case bears on the argument over police use of facial recognition. AI's part in it is hard to weigh. ICE did not mention AI in its release. NBC News reported that new facial recognition and artificial intelligence technology had produced fresh leads in formerly cold cases. Mike Prado of HSI spoke of images enhanced with AI or machine learning. He said that they can give investigators a starting point.[2] ABC News in Australia reported that Clearview AI's facial recognition was used. Forbes reported that officials did not confirm Clearview or any specific program.[3] Crikey reported on 25 January 2024 that Australian case material had been analyzed with Clearview AI. The Australian Federal Police was not allowed to use that software.[4] The outcomes are ICE's count. No figure shows how many identifications came from the tools and how many from manual work. In a separate case in Finland, police were reportedly reprimanded. A unit of the National Bureau of Investigation had allegedly used Clearview AI to identify potential abuse victims.

title: Joseph Coates’s POEMS syndrome went into remission after a stem cell transplant that physicians enabled with three drugs that an early Every Cure algorithm also ranked highly

headline: A man with a rare blood disorder became well enough for a transplant
metric: he responded within one or two weeks
brief: Public money now goes to the search for new uses of old drugs. A patient's case is told in support of that spending.[1] In January 2024 a 37-year-old man from Renton, Washington, was critically ill with POEMS syndrome. He was too sick for a transplant of stem cells. David Fajgenbaum of the University of Pennsylvania and Every Cure recommended three drugs used for multiple myeloma. The patient's hematologist and oncologist, Wayne Gao, agreed to give them. Fajgenbaum later explained that an early Every Cure algorithm had also scored those drugs highly.[2] The patient reported that he responded within one or two weeks. He later received a transplant and reported full remission five months after it. The recovery was reported by several outlets.[3] Mayo Clinic authors published a case series on 31 May 2023. They reported that five of six patients with relapsed POEMS syndrome responded to regimens built on carfilzomib, one of the three drugs. None of them received this combination.[4] The sources include no detailed case report or case-specific model output. Nor do they establish which algorithm or release scored the drugs. The algorithm's part therefore rests on accounts from Fajgenbaum and Every Cure.[5]

title: A 76-year-old reads a transient negative T-wave on his own Apple Watch ECG after gym exercise. Work-up finds silent three-vessel disease. He has quadruple bypass surgery (Amsterdam UMC)
summary: A 76-year-old saw a passing negative T-wave in a recording from his Apple Watch ECG app after exercise. Tests showed three-vessel coronary disease. He received four bypass grafts.
headline: A 76-year-old spots a change on his Apple Watch ECG, leading to a bypass
metric: he received four bypass grafts
brief: In a case report published on 30 January 2024, Koster and colleagues at Amsterdam UMC describe a 76-year-old man with no symptoms. On rare occasions and out of interest, he recorded an electrocardiogram (ECG) in lead I on his Apple Watch right after exercise. In the last of these recordings he noticed a negative T-wave that deepened over about seven minutes and returned to normal after 22 minutes. A cardiologist found that his resting ECG and examination were normal. An exercise test, however, reproduced the change. Imaging then showed three-vessel coronary disease. He received four bypass grafts and recovered uneventfully. The authors report no result from the app's rhythm classifier.[1] The watch recorded the ECG. The patient read it before his doctors did. It is not established whether he would have come to harm without the recording. The authors write that using the watch to document ischemic changes should be studied systematically before it enters routine clinical care.[2] In a study published on 31 August 2020, cardiologists at Magna Graecia University in Catanzaro moved an Apple Watch around the body. In this way they recorded nine-lead ECGs from 100 participants. They reported that these ECGs agreed with standard 12-lead ECGs in identifying changes in the ST segment among patients with heart attacks.[3] This patient recorded lead I alone. The study therefore bears on his case only in part.
system: Apple Watch ECG app (single lead-I recording; its rhythm classifier is not mentioned in the report)
comparator_against: the cardiologist's resting 12-lead ECG and physical examination
comparator_before: A standard ECG was completely normal, as was physical examination.
comparator_after: he noticed immediately after exercise, a negative T-wave that became more prominent in ∼7 min, then slowly returned back to a normal positive T-wave after 22 min

title: A QT measurement on a Withings ScanWatch ECG leads to beta-blocker therapy for congenital long QT syndrome
summary: A Withings ScanWatch displayed a prolonged QT interval that led clinicians in Germany to diagnose inherited long QT syndrome in a father. His daughter had it. Both were prescribed nadolol.
headline: Smartwatch readings lead to a family's long QT diagnosis
metric: displayed values such as QT 506 ms and QTc 457 ms
brief: A man came to the cardiology clinic of University Medical Centre Mannheim, Germany, because of readings from his smartwatch. The visit led to a diagnosis. The man, an asymptomatic 39-year-old, had recorded single-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) on his Withings ScanWatch out of curiosity. The watch displayed a QT interval of 506 ms and a corrected QT interval (QTc) of 457 ms, among other values. Genetic screening showed a previously unpublished KCNH2 variant, which established congenital long QT syndrome. Nadolol shortened his QTc to 430 ms. His 7-year-old daughter, who carried the same variant, was also prescribed nadolol.[1] The case report appeared on 4 July 2024 without dates for the events. The diagnosis rested on clinical ECGs and genetic testing. The authors do not say who first noticed the watch's values. Researchers at University Hospital Basel, who have no tie to Withings, tested the ScanWatch's automated QT measurement in 317 patients. They found that the watch measured QTc automatically in 56% of them. They concluded that its algorithm needed improvement for clinical use.[2]

title: After a smartwatch single-lead ECG captures a 165 bpm wide-complex tachycardia in a 64-year-old man, Emory cardiologists diagnose ventricular tachycardia, which they treat with an implanted defibrillator
summary: A smartwatch ECG function of an unnamed brand recorded a 165 bpm wide-complex tachycardia during palpitations. Cardiologists diagnosed ventricular tachycardia. They implanted a defibrillator.
headline: Emory diagnoses VT after a smartwatch ECG records a 165 bpm tachycardia
metric: recorded a 165 bpm wide-complex tachycardia during palpitations
brief: Authors in the Division of Cardiology at Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta published a case report online on 12 March 2025. They describe a 64-year-old man with a replaced aortic valve. During palpitations he recorded a single-lead electrocardiogram on his smartwatch. The watch flagged a heart rate above 150 beats per minute with a warning to speak to a doctor. Clinicians read a wide-complex tachycardia at 165 beats per minute on the trace. Hospital telemetry then recorded episodes of ventricular tachycardia. Doctors implanted a defibrillator. Three months after his discharge, it shocked him for ventricular tachycardia. After an ablation, later checks of the device showed no further episodes. The watch did not classify the rhythm. The authors note that no smartwatch algorithm is validated to detect ventricular tachycardia. The diagnosis came from clinicians. Neither the brand nor the model of the watch is named. The authors write that his ventricular tachycardia would have gone undiagnosed had his clinician not considered the smartwatch data.[1] On 18 November 2025, cardiologists in Haifa with no tie to the Emory team published a paper online. They cite the case and pool 20 published patients whose ventricular arrhythmias were captured by smartwatches.[2]

title: Smartwatch “heart arrhythmias” alert leads to a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy from premature atrial contractions in a 34-year-old, whose ejection fraction rises from 15% to 50% after ablation
summary: A smartwatch of unstated brand flagged arrhythmias that led to a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy in a 34-year-old man, and radiofrequency ablation restored his ejection fraction to 50% at six months.
headline: A smartwatch alert leads a 34-year-old to treatment for a weakened heart
metric: radiofrequency ablation restored his ejection fraction to 50% at six months
brief: Cardiologists in Thessaloniki published a paper on 19 December 2025. They note that premature atrial contractions are a major source of false-positive alerts for atrial fibrillation on smartwatches.[1] In this case, an alert led to the diagnosis of a heart condition that clinicians could treat. A 34-year-old man with no symptoms saw his primary care physician after his smartwatch detected “heart arrhythmias”. An electrocardiogram showed frequent premature atrial contractions. A cardiologist found an ejection fraction of 35% with a dilated ventricle. Months later, despite treatment for heart failure, imaging showed an ejection fraction of 15%. Radiofrequency ablation stopped the arrhythmia. At six months he was symptom-free with an ejection fraction of 50%.[2] The watch's part is established only as the trigger. The authors do not identify the device or say what form its alert took. The rise from 15% to 50% shows the effect of the ablation.[3]

title: Columbia's STAR system found two motile sperm in a sample that seemed sperm-free in manual checks, so a couple who had tried for 19 years had a girl
summary: Columbia University's STAR system found seven sperm, two of them motile, in 2.5 million images of a “sperm-free” sample. A couple who had tried for 19 years then had a girl.
headline: STAR finds two motile sperm, letting a couple have a girl after 19 years
metric: found seven sperm, two of them motile, in 2.5 million images of a “sperm-free” sample
brief: Columbia University Fertility Center now charges $3,000 for a STAR analysis.[1] The first pregnancy that the center reported with STAR came from a couple who had tried for 19 years to have a child. The husband, who had non-obstructive azoospermia, gave a sample that had been judged sperm-free on manual examination. STAR captured about 2.5 million images of it and detected seven sperm, two of them motile. Embryologists injected the two motile sperm into eggs. The pregnancy test was positive in March 2025. A girl was born in December 2025. The evidence for the method is one peer-reviewed research letter, written by the team that built STAR. The rest consists of figures that the clinic reports about itself.[2] Chia Lin Chang of Chang Gung Memorial Hospital in Taiwan declares no conflict of interest. In September 2026 Chang concluded that the case shows that the method is technically feasible. Chang added that the case cannot count as evidence of clinical efficacy without data from a prospective series of cases.[3] The sources show no test of whether a longer manual search of the same sample would have found the two sperm. STAR cannot help men who produce none.[4]
system: STAR (Sperm Tracking and Recovery): a semen sample flows through a single-use microfluidic chip while a high-speed camera (about 300 frames per second, over 8 million images an hour) images it; an AI object-detection model flags sperm among cellular debris in real time and a microfluidic gate or robotic step diverts each flagged sperm into a droplet for immediate injection or freezing
developer: Columbia University, Columbia University Irving Medical Center (team led by Zev Williams and Hemant Suryawanshi)
deployer: Columbia University, New York (used on its own patient)
domain: Healthcare - reproductive medicine (IVF for non-obstructive azoospermia)
segment: Academic fertility clinic and IVF laboratory
comparator_against: the earlier manual sperm searches and two surgical sperm extractions for the same patient
comparator_before: several manual sperm searches, and two surgical procedures to extract sperm
comparator_after: In about two hours, STAR scanned 2.5 million images, identifying 2 viable sperm cells

brief: A randomized trial has tested ENAD-DET-01, a polyp detector from the South Korean company Ainex. At two Seoul hospitals between May 2023 and April 2025, 998 patients were assigned at random to colonoscopy with or without the system. The system draws a circle on the monitor when it detects a polyp. Adenomas were found in 52.3% of patients with the system and 36.1% without.[1] For sessile serrated lesions and cancers, the difference between the groups was not statistically significant. A control rate of 36.1% left room for improvement. Units that already detect more may see a smaller gain. Elsewhere, researchers found no gain in a randomized trial of computer-aided polyp detection at a Japanese community hospital. Both Seoul hospitals used one Olympus platform, so the trial does not test the system on other equipment.[2] The Korea Medical Device Development Fund paid for the study. The authors report no conflicts of interest.

title: Lynxight alerts lifeguards at Inglewood Pool to an unconscious swimmer who recovers fully after rescue
summary: Lynxight, a camera system at a Perth pool, alerted a lifeguard's smartwatch to a man who had sunk unconscious. Lifeguards rescued him with help from a swimmer. He recovered fully.
headline: Lynxight alerts a Perth lifeguard to a sinking swimmer, who is rescued
brief: On 10 June 2025, a man suffered a medical episode and sank in the outdoor pool at Stirling Leisure - Inglewood in Perth. Lynxight is a camera system built to detect swimmers in distress. It sent a lifeguard a smartwatch alert with the swimmer's location and images. Another swimmer noticed the emergency on his own and lifted the man to the surface.[1] The alerted lifeguard and other lifeguards brought him out of the water. The City of Stirling reports that he was conscious when paramedics took him away. It also reports that he later recovered fully.[2] Help came by two routes. The alert reached a lifeguard who had not seen the man sink.[3] A fellow swimmer noticed him independently. The sources do not show whether he would have survived without the alert.

headline: DeepSeek-R1 flags familial Mediterranean fever, which gene tests confirm
metric: colchicine stopped attacks after ~30 years of symptoms
brief: A 34-year-old man of Egyptian origin had recurrent inflammatory attacks from early childhood. Despite almost three decades of symptoms, extensive investigations had not established a diagnosis. On 28 June 2025 he began a dialogue with the DeepSeek-R1-0528 model. The model refined its differential diagnosis toward familial Mediterranean fever and repeatedly advised specialist supervision. He arranged genetic testing himself. The test showed two pathogenic MEFV variants. He obtained colchicine from an Egyptian pharmacy and took it on his own. His attacks stopped, but his liver enzymes rose and the drug was paused.[1] Colchicine was later resumed at a lower dose under close supervision. In February 2026 he presented to the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, which confirmed the diagnosis. He has remained free of attacks.[2] The model's part was the hypothesis and the suggested work-up. The confirmation came from genetic testing and his response to colchicine. The evidence for the benefit comes from one patient. Two rheumatologists in Istanbul published a study on 31 October 2025. They found that ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok answered patient questions on familial Mediterranean fever best on recovery and follow-up. The same chatbots answered less well on diagnosis.[3]

comparator_before: Despite almost 3 decades of symptoms, extensive investigations, including contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and MRI, gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and urological assessment, failed to establish a diagnosis.

brief: The Department of Justice reported on 30 June 2025 that its analysts and their collaborators had detected anomalous Medicare billing in Operation Gold Rush. According to the department, health agencies stopped all but about $41 million of about $4.45 billion scheduled for payment. The agencies were the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The $4.41 billion that was stopped went into escrow. The Justice Department said that the health agencies intended to seek its return to the Medicare trust fund. In its later announcements, the department does not say what finally became of that money.[1] Medicare supplemental insurers still paid about $900 million. The Justice Department credits the detection to proactive data analytics. In the same release, it announced plans for an AI-enabled Data Fusion Center. According to the American Hospital Association, accountable care organizations had also reported the suspect billing for intermittent urinary catheters. In June 2024 the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services called the 2023 volume of that billing highly suspect.[2] No source shows that AI flagged these claims. None says what share of the hold came from the analytics.[3]

brief: A case report in Resuscitation Plus, published on 12 August 2026, concerns a 69-year-old man who collapsed in ventricular fibrillation while running alone. He was hidden behind a hedge on a dead-end road.[1] On detecting the fall, his Apple Watch automatically called emergency services on 112 and alerted his emergency contacts. Family members began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance crew arrived about 1.5 minutes later and defibrillated him. He made a full neurological recovery. It is a single documented case, and a similar one appeared in an earlier German report. The authors document that the alerts brought his family to him. They cannot show how long he would have lain there without the alerts. That comparison rests on an interview in which a son says that he would not otherwise have found his father so quickly.[2]

title: Mother's AI query prompts a genetic evaluation that leads to a CDC42BPB diagnosis in a 22-month-old
summary: A smartphone app flagged a rare skull finding in a 22-month-old. The authors describe it as powered by Google's Med-Gemini-3D. It led to a genetic diagnosis. The app is unidentified.
headline: Mother's AI query prompts a rare-disease diagnosis in a 22-month-old
brief: In a case report published on 16 January 2026, Hajebian and Friel describe a 22-month-old girl with skull defects. The treating physician did not initially recognize the defects on her computed tomography scan. Her mother ran a three-dimensional reconstruction of the scan through a smartphone app. The authors describe the app as powered by Med-Gemini-3D. The app returned “Catlin mark skull”, a historical name for enlarged parietal foramina. A CDC42BPB variant was then identified on genetic evaluation. The authors state that establishing the diagnosis facilitated earlier therapeutic interventions.[1] The role of AI rests on the authors' description alone. In the abstract, they do not identify the app. Google had said in May 2024 that Med-Gemini was not available for commercial use.[2]
system: Smartphone application described by the authors as powered by Med-Gemini-3D
model_version: Med-Gemini-3D (Google, 2024) per the authors; the app's identity is not verified
deployer: The patient's mother (consumer use)
location: United States (authors at Garnet Health Medical Center, Middletown, New York)
comparator_against: the treating physician's initial reading of the CT scan
comparator_before: symmetric ossification defects adjacent to the sagittal suture that were not initially recognized by the treating physician
comparator_after: suggested a diagnosis of "Catlin mark skull," a historical term for Enlarged Parietal Foramina (EPF)

title: When Meta flags a suicide post on Instagram by an 18-year-old in Raebareli at 8:58 pm, Uttar Pradesh Police reach him within 12 minutes after he took rat poison
summary: Meta's system for detecting suicide risk flagged an 18-year-old's Instagram post for review. Raebareli police reached him within 12 minutes. He was treated after taking rat poison.
headline: Raebareli police arrive in 12 minutes after Meta flags a suicide post
metric: A police team reached his home within 12 minutes
brief: The Raebareli rescue preceded a similar rescue in Meerut in June 2026. Both took place under an arrangement in which Meta has alerted the Uttar Pradesh Police since 2022.[1] On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old posted a suicide video on Instagram. Meta flagged it at about 8:58 pm and emailed the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his phone number and location and alerted Raebareli police. A team reached his home within 12 minutes and found an empty packet of rat poison. Police and family took him to a hospital. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable.[2] None of the sources says whether Meta’s classifier or a user report first flagged the post.[3] No clinician is quoted, and the type of rat poison is not reported. The claim that his life was saved therefore rests on the police account.[4] Meta’s figure for faster escalation is self-reported and dates from November 2017. At that time, the company said that reports accelerated by pattern recognition were escalated to local authorities twice as quickly as other reports.[5]
system: Meta's suicide and self-injury detection and review pipeline on Instagram, with email alerts to the Uttar Pradesh Police Social Media Center at DGP headquarters
deployer: Meta Platforms with the Uttar Pradesh Police Social Media Center (Decode: Uttar Pradesh has been part of Meta's suicide-prevention program since 2022)

metric: 36.5% complete skin clearance with zasocitinib versus 13.9% with deucravacitinib at week 16
brief: In the LATITUDE Atlas phase 3 trial, 36.5% of 301 participants on zasocitinib reached complete skin clearance at week 16. On deucravacitinib, 13.9% of 303 participants did so. Takeda reports these figures.[1] Takeda also reports that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted priority review to its application. No approval had been reported by 29 October 2026.[2] A Cochrane meta-analysis by Sbidian and colleagues, published on 6 August 2025, included an earlier phase 2b trial of zasocitinib. The authors rated the certainty of evidence as low for most comparisons that involve the drug. They declare no ties to Takeda or Nimbus.[3] The attribution to AI is weaker. Nimbus and Schrödinger developed zasocitinib with computational structure-based design. Schrödinger describes free-energy calculations and virtual screening. The approach was AI-assisted, according to a Takeda scientist interviewed in Drug Target Review in 2025.[4] None of these accounts isolates the effect of AI from the rest of the discovery work. Takeda announced an upfront payment of approximately $4 billion for the program when the acquisition closed in 2023.[5] That payment is no measure of the effect of AI.
system: Schrodinger physics-based computational drug-design platform with machine learning, used by Nimbus Therapeutics to discover NDI-034858 (TAK-279, zasocitinib)
deployer: Takeda (clinical development, LATITUDE phase 3 program)
location: United States (Nimbus, Boston; Takeda Development Center Americas, Cambridge, Massachusetts); phase 2b at 55 sites in the United States and Canada
comparator_against: deucravacitinib (Sotyktu), the active comparator in the LATITUDE Atlas phase 3 trial
comparator_before: 13.9% of those receiving deucravacitinib (n = 303)
comparator_after: 36.5% of patients (n = 301) achieving PASI 100 at week 16
value_what: Approximately $4 billion upfront for acquisition of the TYK2 program subsidiary, subject to closing adjustments; a transfer rather than an estimate of AI-created value.

Those counts come from the police. No outside audit of them is known. Police have not said whether Meta's classifier flagged the post or a user reported it. Meta publishes no false-positive data for India. That gap leaves open how often an alert sends officers to someone who was never at risk.[4]
